claims.claim: The American Anthropological Association defines anthropology as 'the study of what makes us human.'
OpenStax's Introduction to Anthropology states that 'anthropology is the study of humanity across time and space.'

In the United States, anthropology is traditionally organized into four fields — cultural anthropology, biological anthropology, linguistic anthropology, and archaeology — which AAA describes as 'the pillars on which the whole discipline rests.'
Most anthropologists specialize in one or two of the four fields while keeping general familiarity with them all.

Anthropology's central narrative holds that human beings developed flexible biological and social features that worked together in a wide variety of environmental and historical conditions to produce a diversity of cultures.

Cultural anthropology is devoted to describing and understanding living cultures: everyday thoughts, feelings, and actions, unspoken norms and values, and larger forces such as economic change and political domination.

Biological anthropology focuses on the origins, evolution, and biological diversity of humans, drawing on fossils, genetics, and the study of living primates; forensic anthropology applies its techniques to human remains in legal and historical contexts.
Linguistic anthropology focuses on language as a primary means by which humans create culture — including how language shapes thought, identity, community, and power.
Archaeology studies the human past through material remains: artifacts (objects made by humans) and fossils, recovered from the ground through careful excavation.

The four fields complement one another, giving a well-rounded picture of what humans share and how we differ across time, space, and social settings; combining insights from the fields produces a richer understanding of issues such as gender, inequality, race, and the environment.

Holism is anthropology's distinctive method of analysis, one that foregrounds the ever-changing relationships among different realms of culture; anthropology ranges across all realms of human thought and activity while other disciplines focus on single realms.
Anthropologists put the four fields to work on real problems; AAA's examples include technology innovation, urban planning, historic preservation, communications strategy, and forensic investigation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the four-field division is universal.
positions: AAA and OpenStax present the four fields (cultural, biological, linguistic, archaeological) as the traditional organization of anthropology in the United States.

Anthropology outside the United States, and some U.S. programs, organize the discipline differently; applied/public anthropology is sometimes treated as a distinct area rather than folded into the four.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson attributes the four-field division to AAA and OpenStax, frames it as the traditional U.S. organization, and avoids claiming universality.
Lesson uses 'biological anthropology' throughout, matching AAA and OpenStax, and does not assert that the older term is wrong.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the four fields always agree.
positions: The four fields are complementary and are kept together because their insights combine.
OpenStax notes candidly that biological and cultural anthropologists do not always agree on the best approach to sociocultural enquiry.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson keeps both facts: complementarity is the organizing ideal, honest disagreement is part of the reality check.

sourceRecords.title: What is Anthropology?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200; the /about/what-is-anthropology/ URL redirects to /practice-teach/what-is-anthropology/, which is registered). Supports: 'Anthropology is the study of what makes us human'; the four fields — human biology, archaeology, cultural anthropology, and linguistics — as 'the pillars on which the whole discipline rests'; that individual anthropologists specialize in one or two fields but keep general familiarity with all; that the approaches complement one another and give a well-rounded picture of what we share as humans and our diversity across time, space, and social settings; applied work ('it's all anthropology') spanning technology innovation, urban planning, historic preservation, communications strategy, and forensic investigation; the integrated food example. Facts synthesized; only the attributed one-line definition and the 'pillars' phrase are quoted.
